title: Trump returns to South Carolina as Senate race tightens
description: President Trump returned to South Carolina - the second time in eight days. The amount of attention and money its U.S. Senate race is getting i
body:
President Trump returned to South Carolina - the second time in eight days. The amount of attention and money its U.S. Senate race is getting is raising questions about how red the state really is.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    JUANA SUMMERS, HOST:  President Trump is crisscrossing the country in the final days before Election Day to stump for Republican candidates. And he went back to South Carolina today for the second time in eight days. Now, that state is known to be ruby red, but the amount of attention and money the U.S. Senate race there is receiving raises some questions about just how safely Republican that seat is. Gavin Jackson with South Carolina Public Radio covered the president's rally in Rock Hill and is with us now. Hey, Gavin.GAVIN JACKSON, BYLINE: Hey.SUMMERS: So, Gavin, you've been reporting on South Carolina politics for a while now. I know because I run into you every time I go to the state. So please just help us all understand what's happening. These last few days before polls close are, of course, so crucial. And the president's making a state he won just two years ago by - let me get this right - 18 points a top priority?JACKSON: Yeah, that's right, Juana. I used to say that we're a red state wedged between two purple states, and while we are still a very Republican state, there are some purple cracks that are appearing. Now, Trump is all-in on Darline Graham, who he urged to run for a full term following her appointment to the position after her brother, Lindsey, died in July. There was a bruising August primary that resulted in fissures that have only gotten bigger, especially among supporters of her runoff opponent, Congressman Ralph Norman, whose backyard this rally was held in. Now, Trump continued attacking Democratic Senate candidate Annie Andrews, who's a pediatrician, and he repeatedly called her by anti-trans slurs, all as he continues to look to boost turnout among these low propensity voters up there.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: A vote for Darline is a vote to cast communists into political oblivion. And...JACKSON: Now, what Trump hopes to accomplish with his second visit here in eight days is to enthuse Republicans and ensure they come home (ph) and not stay home on Tuesday.SUMMERS: All right, so I just want to understand here. It sounds like one reason this race is unexpectedly so competitive has become - is because some Republicans did not get their way. They didn't get their preferred candidate back in the August primary.JACKSON: Simply put, yes, especially some of those Norman hardcore voters - some think it may be easier to replace a Democrat in six years than a Republican named Graham. Now, this situation is so dire that Republican candidates' closing arguments this week have been the need to unify or risk losing the Senate and the House all because of South Carolina. In fact, Texas Senator Ted Cruz told Republicans in Myrtle Beach Monday that Democrats will go after Trump if they take the Senate.Now, besides the unity messaging and Trump coming to town to turn out those low propensity voters, the money is flowing into this race. In fact, NPR's Stephen Fowler crunched numbers and found that in the past month both parties have shoveled about $40 million into the Senate race, and that's according to AdImpact tracking data. So that's four times as much as what was planned a month ago for this Senate race.SUMMERS: OK, got it. I mean, we are really on the home stretch here. Gavin, what are you hearing about how close this race is right now?JACKSON: I mean, look at the polls. Polls show that Graham and Andrews are either tied, like The New York Times/Siena poll, within or just outside the margin of error, like The Citadel's poll on Tuesday. And all this comes as Andrews is peaking at just the right time and is fueling Democrats' dreams of winning a seat they haven't won since 1998. In fact, a Republican pollster I spoke with yesterday is nervous but sees this as a four-point race for Graham, though the write-in Ralph movement, candidate apathy and third-party candidates will really make this closer than ever.SUMMERS: All right, curious to see what happens there. I do wonder, though, is this affecting downballot races in South Carolina too?JACKSON: It actually is, and that's another concern that I'm hearing from folks about, specifically in the 1st Congressional District. That's where candidates are vying to replace outgoing Republican Congresswoman Nancy Mace. And that Lowcountry coastal district was flipped by a Democrat in the 2018 midterms before Mace won it back in 2020. So now Republicans fear that Democrat Nancy Lacore could flip it back, even though that district was bolstered by redistricting in 2022. Again, this is another race where you have a strong Democratic candidate who's capitalizing on this political environment and not leaning all the way into the party but showing an independent streak that's really attractive to South Carolina voters.SUMMERS: South Carolina Public Radio's Gavin Jackson, thanks.JACKSON: Thanks, Juana.(SOUNDBITE OF J. COLE SONG, "FORBIDDEN FRUIT")

title: Democrats seek to weaken the Republican lead in state legislatures
description: The Pennsylvania State Capitol rotunda a
body:
The Pennsylvania State Capitol rotunda as seen last year.
                
                    Aimee Dilger/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Aimee Dilger/AP
    

   
   While races for Congress or governors' mansions may dominate the airwaves, some of the most competitive and significant contests are farther down the ballot.   More than 6,100 seats are up for election in state legislatures, which make most of the laws on education, taxes, reproductive rights, crime and social media access, among other things.   "The fact of the matter is the day in, day out basis, state governments, state lawmakers, state governors have a greater impact on our everyday lives than what takes place in Washington D.C.," said John Kennedy, a political science professor at West Chester University in Pennsylvania.   
   Republicans control the legislature in 28 states, while Democrats have control of 18 legislatures. The remaining four are divided or run under power-sharing deals.   Both parties are sizing up their prospects   Committees for both national parties are picking their races to promote, with Democrats trying to seize on the anti-incumbent mood and low popularity of President Trump.   "By taking advantage of this once-in-a-generation opportunity and environment to build power, we can capture new majorities," said the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee in listing its target districts around the country.   
   The Republican State Leadership Committee acknowledged in an April strategy memo that 2026 poses, "a political environment that is likely to be one of the most challenging for state Republicans in recent years." It said it's taking a "defensive-first posture" to hold onto seats already held by the GOP.   Democrats are pouring millions of dollars into trying to flip Republican-held chambers in several states, especially Wisconsin, Michigan, Arizona, New Hampshire, Minnesota and Pennsylvania.   That would give some Democratic governors greater power to pass their policy priorities or let Democrats block GOP initiatives.   The elections for Pennsylvania's divided legislature highlight the stakes   For example, in Arizona Republicans hold a four-seat majority in the state Senate and a six-seat advantage in the House of Representatives, giving Democrats a chance to take one or both chambers. If they take both, Democratic Governor Katie Hobbs, if she wins re-election, would have an easier time implementing blocked efforts, such as rolling back school vouchers and appointing agency leaders.   
   In other states, Democrats are simply looking to reduce Republican power or break the supermajorities that prevent Democratic governors from vetoing their bills, like in North Carolina and Kansas (if Democrats hold the governor's office there).   The potential for a party shift may be the most pronounced in Pennsylvania, where Gov. Josh Shapiro, a Democrat, is in a constant policy battle with a split legislature where Democrats hold a slim majority in the state House but Republicans hold a four-seat majority in the Senate.   Democrats have not won a trifecta – full control of the state's executive and legislative branches – in more than 30 years. It could come down to the results of a few close state Senate races in the Philadelphia suburbs.   The incumbent Shapiro, running for re-election, is already making a list of what he hopes to accomplish "in the first 30 days" if that happens.   
   "We're going to raise the minimum wage to $15 an hour," he said at a campaign rally. "I'll tell you what else we're going to do – we will codify abortion rights into law in the commonwealth of Pennsylvania. I'll tell you what else we're going to do – we're going to build more affordable housing and take on those utility companies that keep jacking up our rates here in Pennsylvania."   While abortion is legal in Pennsylvania, Democrats want to reduce restrictions and add language that would make it clearer and less subject to judicial interpretation. Republican lawmakers have blocked those moves.   Republican candidate says Shapiro should work more across the aisle   Kennedy said Shapiro would try to do a lot with a Democratic legislature.   "Part of his whole image … has been he's someone who gets things done," he said. "And so I suspect if they have the opportunity, there's going to be nothing short of a very ambitious agenda."   Shapiro's Republican challenger, State Treasurer Stacy Garrity, has accused the governor of using the divided legislature as an "excuse" for not getting things done.   
   "The governor has consistently said … he can't do anything because he has a divided legislature," she said during their only public debate. "Well, that's not what real leadership is. Real leadership -- they call the leaders to the table, and you negotiate."   The winners could use redistricting to reinforce their gains   In other states, Democrats are looking to create a bulwark against the ability of Republican governors to push through legislation. In New Hampshire, they hope to win a majority in the 400-member state House of Representatives, thereby providing a check on Republican Gov. Kelly Ayotte, who's running for re-election.   If Democrats gain ground, it will counter a successful years-long strategy by the GOP. Kennedy explained that the shift toward Republican-held chambers stems from the 2010 midterm cycle, when they made sweeping gains in state legislatures. That gave Republicans the power to solidify their hold through redistricting.   And after the rush of mid-decade congressional redistricting before the 2026 elections, some legislatures might turn toward redistricting their own chambers in the next election cycle.      Carmen Russell-Sluchansky covers politics for WHYY.

title: Justice Department issues subpoenas to California election workers
body:
Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder Dean Logan speaks at a press conference on June 2, 2026. His office confirmed to NPR on Thursday that it received grand jury subpoenas directed at employees last week.
                
                    Patrick T. Fallon/AFP via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Patrick T. Fallon/AFP via Getty Images
    

   
   The Department of Justice issued subpoenas to election workers in Los Angeles in an escalation of tensions with California election officials over the Trump administration's efforts to identify noncitizens on the state's voter rolls.   The Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder's office confirmed to NPR on Thursday that it received grand jury subpoenas directed at employees last week.   
   The confirmation follows reporting that first appeared in the The New York Times that at least two employees at the registrar's office were served grand jury subpoenas with instructions to appear in court on Nov. 4.   In recent weeks, the DOJ sent letters to local election officials in California warning them they could "risk significant federal scrutiny and legal exposure" if they refuse to cooperate with DOJ demands to set aside ballots pertaining to people that federal officials have flagged as "likely" noncitizens.   
   "If persons knowingly tabulate ballots cast by individuals identified by federal agencies as noncitizens, they risk becoming aiders and abettors to a federal crime," the letters warned.   A spokesperson for the Justice Department did not respond to a request for comment about the subpoenas.   It is unclear whether the staff who received the subpoenas are the targets of a criminal investigation at this point.   The news of last week's subpoenas comes a day after a federal judge in California rejected a request by the Justice Department to require California election officials to set aside and stop processing the ballots of thousands of California voters who appear on a list of 20,000 names federal officials say are "likely" noncitizens.   U.S. District Judge David O. Carter found there was no legal basis for the DOJ's demand and the court was not convinced its list was reliable. The judge also raised concerns the effort would disenfranchise eligible voters and create election chaos.   The DOJ is appealing his ruling to the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals.   At a hearing in Carter's courtroom on Tuesday, the judge warned Justice Department officials, "This court believes it would be wise that any threats to state and county elected employees cease immediately."   
   Carter repeated that message in the order he issued Wednesday evening, writing: "The court reiterates what it said yesterday: these threats must stop."   Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder Dean Logan expressed gratitude for Carter's comments in a statement Thursday.   "Judge Carter's admonishment about threats directed at election officials on Tuesday was well placed and appreciated," Logan said. "At every step, the U.S. Department of Justice has taken a confrontational, adversarial approach. Election officials are acting in accordance with state and federal law."   He added: "We will take whatever steps necessary to ensure the safety of our employees and to remain focused on serving the voters of Los Angeles County so they can exercise their voting franchise."

title: Here are the Senate races to watch ahead of Election Day
description: A person walks past a voting sign at the
body:
A person walks past a voting sign at the East Point Library on the first day of early voting on October 13, 2026 in Atlanta, Georgia. Early voting will run from October 13th- 30th with Election Day taking place on November 3rd.
                
                    Megan Varner/Getty Images/Getty Images North America
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Megan Varner/Getty Images/Getty Images North America
    

   
   📲 Get the latest on the midterms & more in the NPR App      When this election cycle began, Democrats were seen as a longshot to pick up the Senate.   That's because so many seats that are up for election are in red states. But as the year has gone on and the war in Iran has continued, the field has widened considerably.   Polling, ad money and candidate and surrogate travel have all indicated competitive races in places Trump won by double digits in 2024. Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio and Texas are all considered Toss Ups, according to the Cook Political Report.   
   "I'm very energized," said Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., chairwoman of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, which is charged with trying to elect Democrats to the Senate. "We have so many candidates running in so many deep red and purple places, and they are winning, and it is exciting. People want change, and we have so much talent on the field right now. I feel very inspired."   The races in all of these competitive states where Trump won are within the margin of error.    
   Republicans have a decidedly different view.   "Senate Democrats' socialist surge has reached a fever pitch, and their desperate conspiracies to defraud voters appear criminal," said Bernadette Breslin, national press secretary for the National Republican Senatorial Committee, the counterpart to the DSCC.   She's referring to a controversy in the Alaska Senate race about the alleged involvement of members of the campaign for the Democratic candidate, Mary Peltola, to recruit Daniel J. Sullivan to run, as first reported by The New York Times. The incumbent Republican is named Dan Sullivan.   "Common-sense voters across red-leaning battlegrounds are preparing to reject the dangerously unaffordable agendas of Abdul El-Sayed [in Michigan], Troy Jackson [in Maine], and Mary Peltola—along with the Democrat Party's dying brand."   
   But showing the direction the winds have been blowing, North Carolina, where Trump won narrowly, and was seen as a Toss Up race at the beginning of this cycle, is now seen as a likely flip for Democrats. And Georgia, once thought to be a top Republican target, is now a likely hold for Democrats.   Even South Carolina, a place Trump won by 18 points, is only leaning toward the Republican Party. Mississippi and Nebraska are also more competitive than Republicans would like, but GOP candidates are favored there.   Democrats need to flip a net of four seats held by Republicans to win control of the Senate. And while the field is wide for Democrats, winning control is hardly a done deal. Republicans have a few targets on the board still, principally in Michigan, but also New Hampshire and Minnesota. Winning even one of those seriously complicates Democrats' math.   The key to whether the Democrats win the Senate and how big the Democratic wave is, if there is one at all, is likely to be Republican turnout. Low GOP turnout could mean the difference between Democrats netting one or two seats and picking up six or seven.    Loading... 
   Let's take a look at the competitive states and where things stand, rated by tiers.   Tiers below are in order of most to least likely to flip. Within tiers, they are in alphabetical order. Ratings are based on the Cook Political Report:    Tier 1: NC (R)   Tier 2: MI (D), OH (R)   Tier 3: AK (R), ME (R), IA (R), TX (R)   Tier 4: KS (R), NH (D), SC (R), MN (D)   Tier 5: MS (R), NE (R), GA (D)   TIER 1: NCNORTH CAROLINA (R-OPEN-Tillis retiring) — LIKELY D   Both parties concede former Gov. Roy Cooper is likely to be the next senator from the state — even President Trump apparently thinks so. "He's going to become your senator," Trump said during a stop in North Carolina earlier this month, "and it's crazy." 2024: TRUMP +3   TIER 2: MI (D), OH (R)MICHIGAN (D-OPEN-Peters retiring) — TOSS UP   Republicans' best pick-up opportunity, this race will test whether a bold progressive can win in a purple state with Democrat Abdul El-Sayed's candidacy. But also factoring in here is former moderate Rep. Mike Rogers' (R) turn to MAGA and use of racist attacks to try and win. 2024: TRUMP +1   
   OHIO (R-Husted) — TOSS UP   Sherrod Brown's (D) decision to try for a comeback after being ousted in 2024 turned this race on its head. He's the challenger, but with his high name recognition and time in the Senate, Republicans have treated him as an incumbent. Trump has tried to boost incumbent Sen. John Husted (R) in recent weeks with explicit comments on his physique. But the issues here have Republicans on the defensive — the economy, gas prices and AI data center growth have given Democrats an opening for a pathway back in a state Trump has won three times. 2024: TRUMP +11   TIER 3: AK (R), IA (R), ME (R), TX (R)   ALASKA (R-Sullivan) — TOSS UP   The hijinks and misinformation ahead of the election here underscore that state's importance. Peltola appeared to have the inside track, but the late recruiting scandal threatens to derail that momentum. 2024: TRUMP +14   IOWA (R-OPEN-Ernst) — TOSS UP   From the governor's race down to the Senate and House race, Iowa looks poised to move left this cycle. Democrat Josh Turek is in a tight race with Trump-backed Rep. Ashley Hinson (R). Tariffs, the war and rising diesel prices have hurt the agricultural economy here and put Republicans on their heels. Plus, Democrats could get be helped by the gubernatorial run of Rob Sand (D), who has run one of the best campaigns of any candidate in the country. 2024: TRUMP +13   MAINE (R-Collins) — TOSS UP   Can Sen. Susan Collins (R) survive again? Polls showed her losing in 2020 and she gutted out a win. The race is tight, and Collins appears to be holding up, but the Democratic base of voters in the only Toss Up state won by Kamala Harris (D) in 2024, gives Troy Jackson (D) a real shot here. 2024: HARRIS +6   TEXAS (R-OPEN-Cornyn lost primary) — TOSS UP   It's hard to see Republicans flipping Michigan and losing Texas, but because of candidate quality in both places, it's possible. State Rep. James Talarico would have probably had a much harder time against incumbent Sen. John Cornyn, but Trump decided to endorse the more MAGA-aligned — and scandal-ridden — state Attorney General Ken Paxton in the primary runoff. That has led to a Brinks truck being backed up into the state of Texas. More than $500 million has been spent on this race since the primary, more than $300 million of that from Republicans. Democrats haven't won statewide in Texas since 1994, there are lots of Republicans here, and Democrats have continued to come up short in recent years even with high levels of enthusiasm, so there's a healthy dose of "believe-it-when-I-see-it" skepticism here. But one thing to consider is that in 2018 when Democrat Beto O'Rourke lost to incumbent Sen. Ted Cruz by less than 3 points, he never led in a single poll. This time around, Talarico has led in almost every one, even if those leads have been within the margin of error. Something to watch: whether Gina Hinojosa's (D) gubernatorial campaign gets close and turns out big numbers of Latinos in South Texas. That could help Talarico over the finish line. 2024: TRUMP +13   
    Loading... 
   TIER 4: KS (R), MN (D), NH (D), SC (R)   KANSAS — TOSS UP (R-Marshall)   Not all Toss Ups are created equal. This has been a surprisingly close race for incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall (R). He's facing a strong challenger in pastor Adam Hamilton and political headwinds because of Trump's policies' effect on the state's economy. Republicans insist Marshall will pull it off at the end of the day and note that Marshall's last race was closer than the lean of the state, too. This is a Toss Up, but the heavy Republican lean of the state makes this one seem less likely for Democrats, but wild things happen in wave years. 2024: TRUMP +16   MINNESOTA (D-OPEN-Klobuchar ran for governor) — LEAN D   One of only three states won by Harris in 2024, and in a year favoring Democrats, Minnesota is perhaps a surprise to be moving more in Republicans' direction in the final days. But Republicans have been trying to peg the lapses in state oversight for a Medicare fraud scandal to Democratic nominee Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan. Plus, Republicans like the race former NFL reporter Michelle Tafoya has been running. This may be a state that tends to vote Democratic but this a place that Hillary Clinton (D) only won by less than 2 points and Harris only won by 4. At the end of the day, the advantage still goes to Democrats here, but it doesn't mean they won't sweat. 2024: HARRIS +4   NEW HAMPSHIRE (D-OPEN-Shaheen retiring) — LEAN D   This has been a top Republican target since the beginning of the cycle when they felt they got a big recruiting win with former Sen. Jon Sununu. And they're hoping for a down-ballot effect with former Republican Sen. Kelly Ayotte favored to win the governorship. But the national political winds still mean Rep. Chris Pappas (D) is the slight favorite. 2024: HARRIS +3   
   SOUTH CAROLINA (R-OPEN-Graham died) — LEAN R   That this one is even being talked about is remarkable. Trump won here by 18 points in 2024 and Sen. Lindsey Graham was heavily favored before his untimely death. Trump pushed for Graham's sister, Darline, to take the seat, but she's a political novice and has been getting swamped on the air with ads boosting Democratic nominee Annie Andrews. Republicans have the edge because of the lean of the state but watch Black turnout here. If it's presidential-level high, Democrats could have a shot. 2024: TRUMP +18   Tier 5: MS (R), NE (R), GA (D)   MISSISSIPPI (R-Hyde-Smith) — LIKELY R   Democrats have been saying for months that this one could be competitive if the political winds get even stronger. That's happened, and they like their candidate. But it would be a shocker if this state that went by more than 20 points for Trump flipped. It's heavily Republican despite its large Black population because white voters vote in extraordinarily high numbers for Republicans here. 2024: TRUMP +22   NEBRASKA (R-Ricketts) — LIKELY R   No one is surprised this cycle by Dan Osborn's independent candidacy. So Republicans are confident this one stays in their hands. But Osborn making this a race at all is an indication of the difficult national environment for Republicans and the kinds of non-GOP candidates that can have an appeal in red states. It's also an example of how bad the Democratic brand is in some of these places, too. 2024: TRUMP +20   GEORGIA (D-Ossoff) — LIKELY D   This was supposed to be a top GOP target but Ossoff's candidacy and his war chest have made him the heavy favorite. Once this one's official, the political world will be waiting for the launch of the Ossoff 2028 campaign. 2024: TRUMP +2

schema.headline: Here are the Senate races to watch ahead of Election Day

title: How powerful is Elon Musk? How his political influence compares to past U.S. moguls
description: Elon Musk listens during an event to mar
body:
Elon Musk listens during an event to mark the launch of the America.gov website, on Sept. 29, 2026, in Washington, D.C.
                
                    Mark Schiefelbein/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Mark Schiefelbein/AP
    

   
   How powerful is Elon Musk?   Consider: Musk has donated more $400 million dollars to Republican causes ahead of this year's midterm elections — far more than mega-donors Michael Bloomberg and George Soros have given to Democrats combined, according to media outlets including The Washington Post and CNN.    This month, Musk's company SpaceX temporarily restricted Ukraine's use of the Starlink satellite system, causing some Ukrainian drones to fall from the sky.   Kara Swisher, the longtime tech journalist and a Musk critic, recently told Morning Edition that no private citizen — and in this case the world's richest person — should be making wartime decisions. David Nasaw, an emeritus professor of history at City University of New York, agrees.   
   "The millionaires, billionaires and now trillionaires have always exercised undue power over the political system," says Nasaw, who has written a biography of Andrew Carnegie, the late 19th century steel magnate. "But there's never been anyone like Musk."   Nasaw notes that Musk was the first person to cross the trillionaire threshold. He also oversaw DOGE, which dismantled the U.S. Agency for International Development, a massive, congressionally created foreign aid operation. Over the years, Musk's companies, including SpaceX and Tesla, have received more than $30 billion in federal contracts, subsidies, loans and tax credits.   "I call it an unholy alliance," says Nasaw. "He makes money and then he returns that money to keep those who are friendly to him in power."   NPR reached out to Musk for comment, but received no reply.   
   Nasaw says the current democratic system can't check someone like Musk, and argues that Congress should pass laws raising taxes on billionaires and limiting campaign spending. Otherwise, Nasaw says: "Democracy is in a death spiral towards oligarchy."   But Richard White, an emeritus history professor at Stanford, says Musk's power isn't unique, historically. In fact, it pales in comparison to J.P. Morgan, the dominant banker of the Gilded Age, which encompassed the final decades of the 19th century. In 1895, Morgan bailed the U.S. out of a financial crisis.   
   "J.P. Morgan thought that he was a co-partner with government," says White. "Once you've saved the United States from having to default on its promise to pay its debts in gold, you realize you have a great deal of influence."   It didn't last. Morgan merged three major continental railroads into a behemoth known as the Northern Securities Company. President Teddy Roosevelt, the trust-buster, knew a monopoly when he saw one and broke it up.   Musk has many critics, but Marian Tupy, a senior fellow at the libertarian Cato Institute, says non-conformists like Musk often lead innovative companies that help drive economic growth. Conformity makes societies stagnant, he says, and a nation needs non-conformists to push scientific and technological advancement.   Tupy also sees political spending as a constitutional right and opposes campaign spending limits, a position he acknowledges is particularly controversial when it comes to the ultra-rich.   "Wealthy accomplished people, having been participants in the global economy and in the American capital system, may actually have better views on what makes the American economy grow than the median voter," Tupy said.   Of course, massive campaign spending doesn't guarantee victory at the ballot box. Musk spent more than $20 million on the Wisconsin Supreme Court race last year, only to see his candidate lose by 10 percentage points.   Musk has benefited during Trump's second term, but if Democrats come to power, White, the Stanford professor, says he could have a tougher time.   "If you had a president and a Congress who were opposed to Musk, they could break him in a year," says White. "SpaceX doesn't exist without government funding."   In fact, he says, Democrats are already talking about investigating Musk if they win the House in next week's midterms.   Musk fired back on X, his social media platform.   "Live by the sword, die by the sword," Musk wrote. "Those who pick fights with me should understand that I will find out who is really pulling the strings and come for them."   
   H.W. Brands, an historian at the University of Texas at Austin, says the debate over the political influence of the super-rich highlights the long-running tensions in American history between democracy and capitalism. Brands, who has written about the industrialists of the Gilded Age, says democracy is based on the idea of equality — including the principle of "one person, one vote," while capitalism is based on inequality. He says people are born with different characteristics and talents and rewarded accordingly.   
   Brands says capitalism surged ahead of democracy in the late 19th century, creating moguls such as Morgan and Carnegie, along with a huge wealth gap. In the early 20th century, progressives responded by breaking up trusts and banning corporate donations to candidates to restore democracy.   Some people see America now in a second Gilded Age with tech and infrastructure titans such as Musk, Jeff Bezos, Mark Zuckerberg and Larry Ellison at the top of the heap. After Trump's two terms, Brands thinks the U.S. is headed for another era of democratic reform.   "I think it's coming over the horizon," he says.

title: 2026 midterm election voter guides: Find local resources in your community
description: Ballot envelopes sit in a bin during the
body:
Ballot envelopes sit in a bin during the processing of ballots for the midterm elections at the King County Elections headquarters on October 23, 2026 in Renton, Washington. Workers have already begun processing ballots in Washington, which uses mail-in voting.
                
                    David Ryder/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        David Ryder/Getty Images
    

   
   We are days away from the 2026 midterms.   Beyond key Senate and House races, the NPR network is following governor races and ballot measures on abortion, LGBTQ+ rights, billionaire taxes, and more.   More from NPR: Here's a look at the 36 races for governor this year   NPR member stations are gathering information for voters — from voter guides down to local races. They offer guides, resources and news reporting from communities across the country to help you be informed for this year's midterm election. title: Alaska's all-important Senate race is roiled by a report on alleged spoiler candidate
description: This combination photo shows Sen. Dan Su
body:
This combination photo shows Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, left, and another Senate candidate named Dan Sullivan.
                
                    Mark Thiessen, Becky Bohrer/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Mark Thiessen, Becky Bohrer/AP
    

   
   Alaska's governor is ordering an investigation after a New York Times report on the state's toss-up U.S. Senate race, which could determine which party controls the chamber next year.   That story detailed efforts by Democratic campaign operatives to recruit what Republicans have long alleged is a spoiler candidate whose presence on the ballot could confuse voters and siphon support from the GOP incumbent. The two candidates share the name Dan Sullivan.   NPR hasn't independently confirmed the Times' reporting, but it's roiled the Senate race just days before Election Day. Democrat Mary Peltola, a former congresswoman, is hoping to flip the seat for her party.   
   The Times' story is based on interviews and communications among Peltola's attorneys and advisers, as well as senior aides at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee.   Democrats have long denied involvement in the non-incumbent Sullivan's candidacy, and both the Peltola campaign and the DSCC reiterated those denials after the Times story published.   While campaigning Wednesday, Peltola called the story a distraction, according to Alaska Public Media, and the non-incumbent Sullivan did not respond to Alaska Public Media's requests for comment. He has previously said it was his decision to run for Senate.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Mary Peltola, a Democrat running for the U.S. Senate seat in Alaska, addresses supporters at an election watch party on Aug. 18 in Anchorage.
                
                    Mark Thiessen/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Mark Thiessen/AP
    

   
   Republicans have pounced on the news.   "Mary Peltola and her campaign have spent months gaslighting Alaskans, denying a scheme they were running all along," Nate Adams, a spokesperson for Sen. Sullivan, said in a statement. President Trump, who tried to overturn his 2020 election loss, called the Alaska findings "Voter Fraud at the Highest Level," in an online post.   Trump's Justice Department had already sought to intervene in the Senate race, asking a court last week to delay certification if the incumbent Sullivan loses by a small margin. The legal effort cited potential voter confusion stemming from the second Sullivan on the ballot.   Election law experts had broadly derided the DOJ's case as weak, in part because the Constitution grants states control over elections.   
   The Sullivan candidacies had already been probed by state officials, but the Alaska Supreme Court ruled in June that the non-incumbent Sullivan could appear on the general election ballot.   Justice Department officials said Thursday the Times' story expands its options for investigating the Senate race, and it filed an amended complaint citing the new reporting.   And in the wake of the Times story, Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy said Wednesday night that he is directing the state's Department of Public Safety to "investigate whether this scheme violated Alaska's laws and whether criminal charges or civil action are warranted."   It's unclear what laws could have been violated.   Trickery has been fairly common in politics, and it can be difficult to write laws that prevent shenanigans, according to Elaine Kamarck, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution who's co-authored a book on dirty tricks in campaigns.   "There's just a lot of tricks," Kamarck told NPR. "There's old ones. There's new ones. In this day and age, the internet makes it really easy to get the word out, both on a trick or, frankly, on a correction to a trick. But it's pretty standard fare for campaigns."   At times major-party advisers will seek to boost third-party candidates, in an effort to undercut the other major-party's candidate. Some voters who spoke with Alaska Public Media compared the new reporting about the Sullivan case to Republican groups' spending in support of a Democrat who's a federal prisoner in New York but who's on Alaska's U.S. House ballot.   
   The second, non-incumbent Sullivan advanced to the general election after Alaska's nonpartisan primary that sends the top four vote-getters to the fall ballot.   Alaska Public Media found mixed reactions to the Times' reporting, with some residents frustrated that it's drawing attention from other issues, and others expressing skepticism that voters would be confused. The ballot notes which Sullivan is the Republican incumbent.   Some experts have pointed out that all the news about the second Sullivan's candidacy could reduce any voter confusion. And because the state has a ranked-choice voting system for the general election, if voters are confused, they could rank both Sullivans and not rank Peltola.   
   Whether voters want to keep the state's unique election system is also on the general election ballot.   NPR's Hansi Lo Wang and Ryan Lucas contributed reporting.

title: Websites pretending to be local news are boosting Democratic candidates
description: Getty Images, Screenshots by NPR/Collage by Emily Bogle/N
body:
Getty Images, Screenshots by NPR/Collage by Emily Bogle/NPR
    

   
   📲 Get the latest on the midterms & more in the NPR App      Ahead of the midterms, some voters are turning to ChatGPT to help them decide who to vote for. When asked for information about candidates in some highly competitive races, NPR found that OpenAI's AI chatbot cited a set of websites that are thinly veiled political ads made to look like reporting from local news outlets.   Less than two weeks before Election Day, when asked "Which House candidates in [Michigan's 4th Congressional District] care about affordability?," the chatbot said Democrat Sean McCann had the "Most detailed published affordability plan" at the very top of its answer. The stakes in this race are high – it's one of the competitive U.S. House races that could determine control of the chamber.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


        
                ChatGPT's response when NPR asked "Which House candidates in [Michigan's 4th Congressional District] care about affordability?"
                hide caption
            
            
   
   As a citation, ChatGPT linked to a website called the Kalamazoo Beacon. The Beacon labels its articles as "news articles" in the website's source code. The outlet also describes itself in the site's source code as "Reporting on Kalamazoo, southwest Michigan, and the issues shaping lakeshore communities."   
   But the Kalamazoo Beacon has only published 16 stories, all about McCann, his policy positions and his record as a state legislator, NPR's review shows.   The Beacon is one of 10 "local news" websites that promote one Democrat apiece in competitive U.S. House races. The 10 sites are part of a larger group of 37 websites identified by the digital security firm VisionHeight that promote many more candidates, mostly Democrats, for a slew of federal, state and local offices, as well as some nonpartisan posts like judges.    ChatGPT's citation of these websites highlights how AI-generated answers can become yet another avenue for stealthy political advertising as more voters consult chatbots before they head to the polls.   While it makes sense that political campaigns and their allies would try to optimize their message for pickup by AI chatbots, pretending to operate as news outlets crosses a line into deception, said Renée DiResta, an associate research professor at Georgetown University who studies online influence campaigns.   When users ask AI chatbots questions, less-credible websites can make an appearance when the chatbots search the internet and summarize the content of links in the search results.   
   "Disclosing funding … would be obviously the ethical thing to do here, or at least indicating that this is a linked effort," DiResta said. At the same time, she said, opposition research entities are trying to make sure that bad information about candidates is found. "So there really is this competition for curation, and it's going to have interesting ramifications as the frontier companies themselves try to figure out how to get better at not falling for it."   It's unclear who operates the websites. NPR was unable to find or reach the site operators. One of the Democrats promoted by the network, JoAnna Mendoza of Arizona, said she wasn't behind the websites and doesn't know who is. The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, the campaign arm of the House Democrats, denied involvement in a phone call with NPR. Other candidates the websites promoted, including McCann, as well as other Democratic super PACs that support the candidates, including American Bridge 21st Century, Tomorrow Together and House Majority PAC, did not respond to NPR's requests for comment.   
   "Local news" websites appear to be part of a larger operation   The set of 37 websites presents candidates in different, overlapping groups. Each of the 10 Democrats covered by a site purporting to cover local news is also the sole subject of a site that offers opinion articles about why voters should support them. The various candidates, who are running in different states, also show up in roundup-style articles on five more websites that have names such as "Public Safety Democrats" and "Democratic Women in the House."    The volume of websites and articles may also help the network's operator boost their preferred narratives, DiResta said.   Another 12 websites, each focusing on a state, covered the House candidates in those states as well as other state and local candidates running for office. The state and national websites also boosted an 11th House candidate that did not have her own dedicated site purporting to be local news.   While most of the sites are openly partisan, the articles published by the network link out to sources for the claims they make, such as congressional voting records, mainstream news articles and partisan news sources, such as the pro-Democrat Courier network.   Opposing candidates mostly made infrequent and brief appearances in articles published by the network that VisionHeight found, NPR's review shows. The articles that did bring up opposing candidates substantively included candidate profiles, as well as writeups that focused on their records on issues that could be possible political liabilities, like support for data centers, not stopping the Iran war, rolling back Medicaid and supporting tariffs.   Multiple indicators suggest that all 37 websites share a common operator. All the websites were set up on September 15 – all but one were registered within an 8-minute period – according to registry and digital certificate data gathered by VisionHeight and Andreas Sjöstedt, a co-founder of Erebus, a hybrid threat forensics firm. Sjöstedt was not involved in VisionHeight's research.   
   Hundreds of articles appeared on the websites in batches in September and October. The large volume of articles in a concentrated amount of time suggests that the operator may have used AI to fill out the material, VisionHeight's report said.   
   After the websites went online, their operator continued to polish them. Earlier in October, the 10 websites that posed as local news outlets, including the Kalamazoo Beacon that had promoted Sean McCann, shared the same description: "Straight local news - reports on the race and (once a content-sourcing workflow exists) community storylines, in neutral third-person news style." Since then, those descriptions have become more tailored to the areas the outlets purported to cover.   How ChatGPT cited the sites   The websites transparently welcome AI chatbots: All the websites explicitly allow a long list of AI crawlers made by major AI companies to scrape information off of them. Many articles are formatted as questions and answers, which chatbots tend to prefer to cite. Many news organizations prevent such crawlers from going through their websites because the crawlers take content without bringing in revenue.   Every website in the network also contained a file called llms.txt, which lists articles on the site in plain text. This is surprising because most websites don't have these files, said Alisha Ukani, a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Washington's Center for an Informed Public, who noticed these files while reviewing the sites at NPR's request. Ukani focuses on how AI is changing the internet. In an email, she noted that the websites that do have llms.txt files tend to be "biased towards technology and business-related websites."   To gauge the group's success in getting picked up by AI chatbots, NPR drafted 37 questions and used them on ChatGPT and Gemini, the two most popular AI chatbots, as well as Google search, which sometimes provides AI-generated answers in its results. For each of the 10 congressional races, NPR asked more general questions, such as which candidates care about issues such as public safety. NPR also asked the chatbots questions more specific to individual candidates, such as their priorities.   
   In 19 responses, or about half the time, ChatGPT cited at least one article from the network of websites, often citing them alongside other sources such as Ballotpedia, a website that tracks races and candidates, or the candidates' own campaign websites. In 17 of those 19 times, the chatbot cited one of the outlets that pretended to be a local news site. In the other two instances, ChatGPT cited websites from the network that purport to cover politics in a state.   The group's output may have been even more successful in being picked up when users ask about down ballot candidates. NPR identified five city council candidates in Michigan that a website in the group called the Wolverine State Report covered. When NPR asked ChatGPT about the positions of each of the candidates, ChatGPT cited the website every time.   Unlike traditional search engines, submitting the same question multiple times to a chatbot can give users significantly different responses. NPR submitted each query only once, so future or parallel experiments may yield different results. However, preliminary research has shown that chatbots tend to cite questionable sources more often when there are very few sources of credible reporting, such as downballot races where there is often less news coverage. The phenomenon is called a "data void."   Google's products behaved very differently. Gemini did not cite any links from the group of websites in all the responses. In seven instances, the chatbot also declined to respond to the questions at all and pointed NPR to external sources. Google search also did not surface any links from the group in its first page search results, and its AI Overview did not mention the websites either.   VisionHeight's report showed that in early October, at least one site did show up on Google's first page result, ranking higher than Ballotpedia. The company did not systematically measure how the sites showed up for different candidates, VisionHeight's CTO Nitsan Daniel told NPR.   
   Google spokesperson Davis Thompson said that the company detected a policy violation in this instance and took "swift action."   "Our generative AI features are built on Search ranking systems, which are designed to show high quality content and block spam and abuse," Thompson said.   OpenAI spokesperson Nate Evans said, "ChatGPT's search tools cite from a range of sources so people can explore and make their own judgements." He added that, "When issues are brought to our attention, we take action to improve our model responses."   It's unclear what OpenAI has changed since NPR flagged the sites to it. The Kalamazoo Beacon was still cited as a source every time after NPR received OpenAI's response and ran a query five times. In some instances, McCann no longer gets the distinction as having the "most detailed affordability plan," but in other instances, he still does.   Thinly veiled advertising that purports to be a news source has a long history, said Patrick Warren, a professor at Clemson University's Media Forensics Hub. People used to get ad flyers that look like newspapers, or glance at ads mixed in with legitimate news in traditional online search, Warren said, and reading AI chatbot answers without evaluating the underlying sources is just the latest version of the experience. "There's nothing new under the sun."   Methodology:   To better understand the content of the websites and how they changed, NPR downloaded every website homepage and article page twice, on October 19 and October 24, which enabled NPR to see how they evolved. These records were also used to verify VisionHeight's observations. NPR manually reviewed all the "local news" and "local opinion" sites and used AI to analyze every article posted on the sites focused on state and national races.   For every candidate mentioned in the articles, AI was used to extract the names, party affiliation and offices in contention. NPR then conducted keyword searches and manually reviewed articles to examine how opposing candidates were portrayed and confirm findings.    To test whether ChatGPT, Gemini and Google search cited the websites, NPR entered the following prompts:    
   Which House candidates in [district] care about affordability?Which House candidates in [district] care about public safety?Tell me about the priorities of women candidates in the House race in [district]?What are the priorities of [candidate] running in House district [district]?   NPR substituted [district] and [candidate] with the 10 candidates and districts the websites focused on. In some races there was either no female candidate or the woman wasn't one who was being promoted by the network.    NPR ran the queries manually on October 22 and 23, using a VPN to change the IP address to the corresponding state or a nearby state. NPR also used individual private browsing sessions for each tool and prompt.

title: For voters from immigrant families and new citizens, voting is bigger than themselves
description: Nicole Solis-Sison on the day she became
body:
Nicole Solis-Sison on the day she became a naturalized citizen. Solis-Sison first came to the U.S. from the Philippines when she was 7.
                
                    Courtesy of Nicole Solis-Sison
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Courtesy of Nicole Solis-Sison
    

   
   Nicole Solis-Sison moved to America when she was seven years old. Her parents and immediate family were fleeing the Philippine government and sought asylum in the U.S.   When they landed in Los Angeles, Solis-Sison thought their stay would be temporary. Eventually, once things calmed down in her home country, they would return. That wasn't the case.   "The Philippine government pursued us in international immigration territory and demanded that we be sent back," she told NPR.   That's when an agent with the then-Immigration and Naturalization Services agency — which has since been renamed Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE — showed up to her house. They were prepared to be deported. But after the agent interviewed her family, they weren't packing their bags back to Manila.   
   "This particular INS [Immigration and Naturalization Services] agent suggested that we should file for asylum, given that we were on U.S. soil," Solis-Sison said.   An immigration agent, Solis-Sison said, gave her family the tools needed to stay in the U.S. legally. Earlier this year, after more than two decades navigating the immigration system, she became an American citizen. Now, at the age of 34, Solis-Sison is voting in her very first election in New York City.   "This is like such a milestone year for me that I'm a first time voter. I created my own voter guide and voter diary," she said.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Ahead of voting in her first election in 2026, Nicole Solis-Sison made herself a voter guide and election diary.
                
                    Courtesy of Nicole Solis-Sison
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Courtesy of Nicole Solis-Sison
    

   
   Many young voters, including Solis-Sison, are worried about their future. Will they be able to buy a home? How will they pay off their student loans? Is it economical to start a family?   But this midterm election, the motivation for voting is a little different for some young people with immigrant family members and for newly naturalized citizens.   Solis-Sison considers herself lucky. As she heads to the polls for the first time, she said her immigrant experience is informing her vote. She feels a responsibility.   "I feel like I do have a weight to protect people who are going through this process, who are getting left behind and harmed because when I tell you, I've only gotten out of it with like a sliver of hope," she said.   
   The power of voting   Juan Escalante didn't know he was undocumented growing up in south Florida.   Originally from Venezuela, his family moved to the states when he was 11 years old. He said he lived a normal life in America but that changed when he discovered he wasn't legally allowed to be in the U.S. around his junior year of high school.   "Basically, what ended up happening was that my parents paid for a lawyer who gave them really bad advice and not only gave them bad advice, but also mishandled their immigration case entirely," Escalante said.   He added when something happens like that, the immigration application can't simply be refiled, "you're kind of out of the line entirely." His immigration status changed under the Obama administration when the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals, or DACA, program was established.   Under the program, he became the first person in his family to graduate college. Then, in 2025, he became the first American citizen in his family. This year, at 37, he will vote in his first general election.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Juan Escalante became a U.S. citizen in 2025, the first in his family.
                
                    Courtesy of Juan Escalante
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Courtesy of Juan Escalante
    

   
   "Being a first time voter here in the United States is something that's profoundly personal and emotional for me because I understand the power of what a vote can do in service of the greater good, in service of the community, in service of the of the future that you want to see for your community, your state and your country."   "I'm proud to be an American citizen," Escalante said.   When he first received his mail-in ballot, Escalante had mixed emotions. He was thrilled to cast a vote, but as a California resident, he found himself overwhelmed by the sheer size of his ballot. But that didn't stop him from meticulously researching every last ballot proposition and candidate. To him, it's something he's worked the majority of his life for.   
   "Despite the amount of bubbles that I had to fill in and the amount of research that I had to do, I never once took that for granted as I was filling out my ballot," he said.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Juan Escalante voted for the first time in the 2025 California special election on redistricting and framed his "I Voted" sticker.
                
                    Courtesy of Juan Escalante
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Courtesy of Juan Escalante
    

   
   But he did want to make sure that his vote supported his family and community. Though his parents are both green card holders, he said it doesn't stop anyone in the family from worrying about their future status. So, when he was spending tons of time trying to figure out which politician to vote for, immigration was at the top of his mind.   "I do want to make sure that my values as an immigrant, as the first of my family to vote and also as a Latino to make sure that all of that is carried and translated through to my ballot," he said.   Mixed status families   24-year-old Deisy España of Wisconsin also feels the weight of her family's immigrant history. España is from a mixed-status family. While she was born in the U.S. and has always been a citizen, her parents are from Mexico. Growing up, both of her parents were undocumented.   España said she didn't understand the risks to her parents when she was younger, like when her parents got pulled over by the police while driving.   "My mom would start, like, doing the sign of the cross or praying and I never understood what that fear was until I got much older and realized that they were scared that they were going to get turned over to ICE," she said.    
   Some of that has changed. Her mom recently obtained a green card. But the fear hasn't completely dissipated. ICE has been in the news a lot since President Trump returned to office. Every time España encounters someone whose family member has been taken by ICE, or reads about an ICE related death, the same thing runs through her head.   "That could have been my dad," she said.   Immigration policy has always been a priority for España and she has always been politically active, despite not being old enough to vote until 2020. But she said more feels at risk this election, especially with Trump's hardline stance on immigration and ICE agents arresting people who look like her parents. España said she carries more than just her views into the ballot box.   
   "I'm voting for my parents. I have to do it for my parents who can't vote. But even now, more than ever," España said.   That has been España's message for other young voters with immigrant families. Don't vote for yourself. Vote for your parents.   23-year-old Leydi Gonzalez of Texas is in a similar position as España. While she is an American citizen, both of Gonzalez's parents are from El Savador. She said the number one thing she was looking forward to once she turned 21 years old was helping her parents gain legal status.   "When I turned 21, the first thing that I was excited for was to finally petition my parents. It wasn't drinking," she said.   Now, thanks to Gonzalez's sponsorship, they have authorization to be in the U.S. They're in the system and crossing their fingers for residency approval.   While there is a layer of legal protection for her parents, Gonzalez is still worried something could happen. Gonzalez said her family started having conversations about who would take care of her siblings if her parents were detained or deported when Trump was first elected president.    
   "That is a scary conversation to have. Like, 'Hey, just in case something unknown happens to your parents, this is who you're gonna be left with,'" Gonzalez explained.   Now, she feels like the stakes are just as high, if not higher. Her community has been rocked by the killing of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Texas by an ICE agent. But she does think things are on the precipice of change this election, especially if control of Congress changes.   It's playing out in her backyard. There is a high profile U.S. Senate race in Texas. While Texas is a reliably red state, Democrat James Talarico has been polling ahead of Republican nominee, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton.   
   She said she is voting for her best interest, but it is bigger than that.   "It definitely feels like I'm voting for my family," Gonzalez said. " Definitely a sense of security for my family."

schema.headline: For voters from immigrant families and new citizens, voting is bigger than themselves

title: 'Affordability? For who?' Voters decide between helping homeowners or public services
description: Volunteers with Florida Rising, a progre
body:
Volunteers with Florida Rising, a progressive nonprofit that organizes residents to take political action on state and local issues, knock on doors in Jacksonville, Fla., to encourage residents to vote no on an amendment that would cut property taxes.
                
                    Malcolm Jackson for NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Malcolm Jackson for NPR
    

   
   JACKSONVILLE, Fla. – The ramp was steeper than she expected, but Rachel Dues was not going to stop. Not mere steps away from what she believed to be the most important thing she would do this year.   Dues, 54, gathered herself then pushed hard, propelling the wheelchair that carried her injured niece to the polls.   "You're gonna get in there. I don't care how," Dues said, her voice breathless with effort. She was speaking as much to herself as she was to her niece, 21-year-old Rochelle Covington, who asked to come along to vote.   
   "By any means necessary," Dues said, giving the wheelchair another shove.   For Dues, this year's midterm election feels existential. Gas prices have soared, her rent is up, and some days it feels like simply buying groceries or paying her electricity bill could push her over budget.   While political candidates all over the country have paid lip service to issues of affordability, here in Florida, the question of how to make life more affordable is literally on the ballot.   A massive property tax cut has been put to voters in the form of Amendment 3, a ballot measure that asks Florida residents to vote on increasing the amount of money that can be exempted from homestead taxes. The proposal would increase the allowable amount from $50,000 to as much as $250,000 over the next two years, cutting billions of dollars in revenue from local governments' budgets. If the measure passes, some jurisdictions could functionally eliminate all non-school homestead property taxes over time.   That could mean thousands of dollars in annual savings for some homeowners — something supporters have called a game-changer for Florida residents stretched thin by a strained economy. But in an already tax-averse state — Florida famously does not have individual income or estate taxes, among others — local governments have limited revenue streams from which to pull funds for public services, and property taxes have been a lifeline.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Rachel Dues, a volunteer with Florida Rising, worries about the prices of rent, food, electricity and gas all increasing this year.
                
                    Malcolm Jackson for NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Malcolm Jackson for NPR
    

   
   Critics have cautioned that the proposed tax exemption will have dire consequences: cuts to public services and infrastructure, eroded social safety net programs and a domino effect that could drive up costs elsewhere should city and county governments attempt to recoup lost revenue.   
   "One of the things our members are always knocking on doors and asking is: affordability? For who?" said Steven Johnson, an organizer with grassroots nonprofit Florida Rising, which organizes residents to get involved in political action on state and local issues.   Florida isn't the only place where politicians have explored ways to cut, or even eliminate, property taxes — 11 states have reined in property taxes so far in 2026, according to an analysis by the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities. But Florida's proposal, which is more expansive than many others, puts the question directly to voters.   
   How they vote, experts said, could set the stage for what's to come in Florida and around the nation.   A disabled veteran, Dues works as a notary and closing agent on home sales. For her, she said, the Amendment 3 vote is personal.   "Lucky for me I'm a resourceful person, but I rely on things like food pantries and other services to get by," Dues said. "Now I'm wondering, what am I going to do if they get rid of all that? What can I do?"   The impact     Since it was introduced, Florida's proposed Amendment 3 has been pitched to voters as an affordability fix for homeowners.   While the state already has laws limiting how much can be taxed of a home's assessed value — and how much that amount can grow each year — this amendment would, in some cases, virtually eliminate all property taxes due on a homeowner's primary residence.   Backers like Florida's Republican governor, Ron DeSantis, and the Florida Realtors trade association have said property taxes have grown out of control and local governments are flush with excess revenue as a result.   "Homeowners have funded the incredible increase in revenue that is now at record growth, and as property values have increased that growth has translated into significant revenue gains for local governments," said Margy Grant, the CEO of Florida Realtors, which as of the end of October put $19.5 million into the 'Vote Yes on 3' campaign. "This is about making sure that Floridians who want to stay in their homes and are seeing this rising cost get to stay in their homes."   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Florida's Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis speaks at an event on Sept. 1 in Tampa. He and the Florida Realtors trade association have encouraged voters to approve Amendment 3.
                
                    Joe Raedle/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Joe Raedle/Getty Images
    

   
   In the campaign to persuade Floridians to vote yes, ads highlight just how expensive daily life has gotten.   
   "Everything keeps going up!" the Vote Yes on 3 website exclaims. "Cost of living. Inflation. PROPERTY TAXES. What if there was a SOLUTION that could help?"   "Florida families are paying more for nearly everything, whether it's groceries, fuel, insurance, utilities and housing," Grant said. "This is tax relief money that stays in a Floridian's pocket instead of going to the government."   Property tax revenue collected by local governments in the state has nearly doubled from around $32 billion in 2019 to almost $60 billion in the last fiscal year, according to the governor's office. Much of that growth, experts said, was driven by a post-pandemic real estate boom with out-of-state residents moving in and low interest rates driving new property sales.   
   The question of how law enforcement, fire and emergency medical services will be affected by these potential tax cuts have fueled headline-grabbing debates across the state. Some public officials have insisted emergency services will be able to weather any cuts, while others, including the Florida Sheriffs Association, warned they would suffer.   Amendment 3 proponents said these warnings have been overblown.   "That is just a talking point of the opposition," Grant said.   Sen. Rick Scott (R-Fla.), who supports the measure, wrote in a post on X that "every county has waste to cut," and argued that the amendment would force local governments to eliminate waste rather than essential services.   But local leaders said services other than police, fire and EMS are likely to be hit even harder: Funds for libraries, public transportation, infrastructure, homelessness prevention, small business supports, after-school programs for kids and more could be eliminated.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Mike Weinstein, Jacksonville's chief administrative officer and a former state legislator, speaks in 2024. Weinstein, a Republican, says Amendment 3 would devastate public services in Jacksonville.
                
                    Bob Self/Florida Times-Union/USA TODAY Network via Reuters
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Bob Self/Florida Times-Union/USA TODAY Network via Reuters
    

   
   The amendment was put to voters "very, very quickly and without understanding the unintended consequences," said Mike Weinstein, Jacksonville's chief administrative officer and a former state legislator. "There's a small segment of homeowners that will benefit from this. But the majority of people — renters, business owners, everyone else, and even many homeowners — won't see any benefit from this amendment at all." (The amendment would limit which homeowners qualify for the increased exemption based on when they purchased their home.)   According to an analysis by the state's Office of Economic and Demographic Research, the amendment would cut local revenue in the state by nearly $12 billion on a recurring basis. In Jacksonville, the Florida Policy Institute found, that could mean losing as much as $372 million over the next five years.   
   "Our budget here is $2 billion. A billion comes from property taxes," Weinstein said. "So, mosquito control, road surfacing, libraries, parks, all will be affected. And so will police and fire."   Weinstein, a Republican, said in lieu of funding things like parks and libraries, fixing roads or clearing trash, the city may instead have to channel resources toward opening a "very big" complaints department.   Getting out the vote    Maggie Fernandez, 68, is exactly the kind of person who might benefit from Amendment 3. She owns her own home. Her husband is retired.   
   But in recent weeks, Fernandez has spent her nights and weekends in the lead up to Election Day phone banking and knocking on doors to get her neighbors to vote the amendment down.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Florida Rising volunteers Maggie Fernandez (left) and Tia Bell-Williams pose for a portrait after a day of canvassing in neighborhoods around Jacksonville. Fernandez, a homeowner, is encouraging voters to say 'no' on Amendment 3.
                
                    Malcolm Jackson for NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Malcolm Jackson for NPR
    

   
   "Sure, I might see some relief in taxes," Fernandez said. "But overall this is going to hurt local services. It's going to hurt people who are worse off than we are."   Fernandez signed up to do voter outreach with Florida Rising. On a recent weekday evening, she was one of more than a dozen volunteers who packed into the progressive nonprofit's office and hit the phones. All told, organizers said, they made nearly 1,500 calls that night.   With early voting already underway in Florida, Fernandez said she felt a renewed sense of urgency to get the "vote no" message out.   She dialed number after number — 111 in one night — leaving messages and urging those who answered to consider how Amendment 3 might hurt their neighbors in the long run.   Down the hall, Dues was also making calls.   When a woman answered halfway through the evening, Dues scrambled for her script.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Florida Rising made door hangers to leave on residents' doors, encouraging them to vote no on Amendment 3, a proposed increase to Florida's property tax exemption.
                
                    Malcolm Jackson for NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Malcolm Jackson for NPR
    

   
   "Amendment 3 may lead to cuts on local services like flood prevention, road maintenance, public transportation and housing assistance and that's what it doesn't tell you when you see those commercials on TV," Dues said. "It doesn't tell you any of that, it just makes you think it's this great amendment."   
   The woman on the other line said she'd be voting no.   Dues exhaled as she hung up the phone.   'People don't know'   Dues doesn't need to work hard to picture how the amendment might affect her daily life. She thinks about it constantly: On her drives across town as she calculates the amount of gas it might take to get home; on her regular visits to food pantries, where she gathers enough bread and eggs and frozen meat to make it through the month.   Will the food banks be able to operate if they lose city funding, she wonders. Will relief programs that help renters like her pay for utility bills or avoid eviction disappear?   In her work as a closing agent, Dues sees how much people are paying to become homeowners in Florida, and, she said, she feels for anyone who is struggling to make ends meet.   But she's done her research and practiced her pitch. Whenever she gets the chance, she tells homeowners that the affordability Amendment 3 promises isn't all it's cracked up to be.   "When I first heard about it, I was like, oh that's great. That'll really help people," Dues said. "But then I learned more about it and it felt like a bait and switch. It might be great for some people, in the short term, but in the long run, it's going to do a lot of harm."   If local lawmakers shift the financial burden into other taxes homeowners could end up paying more in other places, she tells friends and colleagues.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Rachel Dues works as a closing agent and sees how much people are paying to own a home in Florida.
                
                    Malcolm Jackson for NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Malcolm Jackson for NPR
    

   
   Renters like her, she says, may absorb increases put to landlords or commercial properties. And any programs that exist to help people survive won't necessarily be there to help anymore.   The amendment needs the approval of a supermajority — 60% or more — to pass.   
   On a recent morning outside a church on the west side of Jacksonville, Dues got in line to register for the food bank. She needed a few staples, she said, to carry her through the end of the month.   "Are you voting?" she asked the woman working the sign-in desk.   The volunteer squinted up at her.   "You know to vote 'no' on Amendment 3, right?" Dues pitched, taking a number.   Dues said she's never been more nervous before an election.   "It's kind of scary to me that people don't know" about the amendment, she said.   Looking around the crowd gathered for boxes of bread and other pantry items, Dues shook her head.   "How do they expect poor people to be able to live as regular people?" she wondered aloud.   The number in her hand read 104. All around her, the crowd was still growing.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Florida Rising volunteers canvass a neighborhood in Jacksonville, Fla.
                
                    Malcolm Jackson for NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Malcolm Jackson for NPR

schema.headline: 'Affordability? For who?' Voters decide between helping homeowners or public services
